title: How Classified Information Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how classified information works in the United States: the origins of secrecy rules in ancient state secrets and the 1911 Defense Secrets Act, the 1917 Espionage Act and its wartime harshness, the 1869 General Order No. 35 on cameras at forts, Brigadier General Arthur Murray's push for tiered classification, Franklin Roosevelt and Truman executive orders, the atomic age and Leslie Groves's Manhattan Project compartmentalization, the Atomic Energy Act of 1946, the classification levels (top secret, secret, confidential, restricted) and sensitive compartmented information, original versus derivative classification and the scale of classified documents, declassification rules and Obama's Executive Order 13526, the problems of over-classification (corruption, authoritarianism, Manhattan Project secrecy, 9/11 information sharing, leaks, whistleblowers, hiding embarrassments and corporate regulation), and proposed fixes such as time limits, higher standards, accountability, and easier declassification. The episode closes with a listener mail message from court reporter Linda Davidson.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about TV shows and movies, then introduce classified information as a dense topic: governments keep secrets, and the system is bureaucratic and often anti-democratic.

segments.title: History of state secrets and early US secrecy laws
segments.summary: Secrets existed in ancient times but were easier to keep before technology and bureaucracy. Executive orders set classification rules and Congress set punishments, starting with the Defense Secrets Act of 1911, which became the Espionage Act. The vagueness of classification standards is discussed. The 1917 Espionage Act was harsh during wartime, used against Eugene Debs, and later used against the Rosenbergs, Chelsea Manning, Reality Winner, and Edward Snowden.

segments.title: Early military classification and General Order 35
segments.summary: In 1869 the War Department issued General Order No. 35 banning photographs of forts. Brigadier General Arthur Murray complained that everything was stamped confidential and asked for a tiered system. The British four-tier system was considered but rejected, and the hosts joke about classification level names.

segments.title: Atomic age, Manhattan Project and Leslie Groves
segments.summary: Franklin Roosevelt's executive order codified military classification levels. The atomic age raised stakes, and scientists kept their research quiet. General Leslie Groves controlled secrecy on the Manhattan Project through compartmentalization, and his rules shaped the Atomic Energy Act of 1946, along with derivative classification and the early idea of declassification.

segments.title: Executive orders and the classification levels
segments.summary: Truman created the top secret category in 1951 and Executive Order 10290 extended classification power to much of the executive branch, later cut back in 1953. The system settled on top secret, secret, confidential, and restricted. Agency-specific labels such as sensitive but unclassified are noted, and the hosts explain how sub-paragraph markings work in documents.

segments.title: Original vs derivative classification and scale of secrecy
segments.summary: Original classification is done by a small number of officials, while more than four million people with clearances make derivative classifications. Cabinet-level agencies classified over 55 million documents, and the intelligence community classifies petabytes of data each year. Declassification rules, including automatic declassification after ten or twenty-five years, are described as vague.

segments.title: Sensitive compartmented information and Obama's 2009 order
segments.summary: Sensitive compartmented information is a level above top secret, limited to those with specific need. Executive Order 13526 from 2009 replaced earlier orders, set the top secret, secret, and confidential levels, and defined damage levels such as grave, serious, and damage. It lists eight types of information that can be classified.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break in the episode.

segments.title: Problems with over-classification
segments.summary: Over-classification is discussed as a problem: classifying menus and a supposed plot against Santa Claus, the risk of corruption and authoritarianism, the Manhattan Project tipping off the Soviets, 9/11 information-sharing failures, leaks used against political enemies such as Valerie Plame, whistleblower protections, and the Espionage Act's threat to people who leak wrongdoing. Irwin Griswold said over-classification is widespread and often hides embarrassments. Estimates say 10 to 90 percent of classified material may be over-classified. The FCC and Department of Agriculture examples show corporate and public-health information being shielded. Hiding the CIA's secret prisons and torture program kept the public from debating them.

segments.title: Proposed fixes and related episodes
segments.summary: Proposed fixes include time limits on classification, a higher bar for what qualifies, accountability for over-classifiers, and making declassification a real practice rather than relying on FOIA requests. The hosts note an earlier episode on FOIA and mention the film The Card Counter.

segments.title: Listener mail from court reporter Linda Davidson
segments.summary: Listener Linda Davidson, a California court reporter, writes about her career, the need for more court reporters, and the sketch artist work seen in recent trials. The hosts thank her.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and invite email to the show.
